Walking home through the Saturday market in Sehore, Wasim was deep in a chat about the cricket match, thumbs flying. He was looking straight ahead between messages, or thought he was.
"Wasim! Pit!" Devika grabbed his bag and yanked him back.
He stopped a step from an open drain, its cover lifted for repairs, a red cloth tied on a stick beside it.
"I was looking," he said, heart hammering. "I didn't see it."
"You were looking at the road with your eyes and at the match with your brain," Devika said.
A cyclist rang his bell right behind them, and Wasim jumped. He hadn't heard that either.
He put the phone in his pocket. "I'll reply at home." For the rest of the walk he noticed everything: the drain, a cow, a bicycle, the fruit seller calling out prices.

qa.a: A red cloth tied on a stick was beside the open drain.

qa.a: Wasim felt shaken and startled, his heart hammering, because he thought he had been looking.

qa.a: To put the phone away and reply at home, so attention stays on the road while walking.

Last month I learned something about my own brain that still scares me. I'm Dilnaz, and I'd had my licence for five months.
Anjali and I were driving back from college. My phone rang: my mother, about dinner. I put it on speaker, both hands on the wheel, eyes on the road. I thought I was being responsible.
At the zebra crossing near the vegetable market, a man with a cart was already halfway across. In plain view. I didn't see him. Anjali screamed my name and I braked hard. We stopped with a foot to spare.
My eyes had been on the road the whole time. My attention had been on dinner.
I pulled over, shaking, and told my mother I'd call back. Since then I have one rule: phone on silent in the glovebox before I start the car. Not because I'm careless. Because my attention can only be in one place.

Dear Mridul,
Congratulations on the new job and the new scooter! Since you asked for advice, here are three things I learned the hard way.
One: the phone goes in the seat box before you start the scooter. Not on silent, not in your pocket. Last year a message lit up my screen, I missed a turn and nearly clipped a school van. Nothing happened, but it could have.
Two: when someone important is talking to you, your boss, a client, Amma, put the phone face down and look at them. You'll hear twice as much.
Three: anything that can really go wrong, like the salary sheet or a client's payment, gets checked by a second person. I ask my colleague to check mine, and I check hers. No shame in it. Tired eyes miss things.
You'll be great. Call me on Sunday, but not while riding!
Your Bhaiya,
Yash

Ojas, you asked what one habit I'd tell every young worker. I'm Tarun, I supervise electrical work on building sites, and my habit is simple: some moments get my full attention, and the phone isn't invited.

Last year I became a team lead, and in my first month I noticed something odd in our Monday meetings. I'm Kunal, and I'd look up from my notes and see six laptops open, six faces lit blue, fingers typing. Farida would ask a question and three people would say, "Sorry, can you repeat that?"
The meetings were an hour long. Nothing got decided. Everyone was half there.
I didn't give a speech about respect. I tried an experiment. I cut the meeting to twenty minutes and made one rule: laptops closed, phones face down, except for the person taking notes. If you don't need to be there, skip it and read the notes.
The first week felt awkward. People didn't know where to look. By the third week we were deciding things in fifteen minutes and leaving early. Farida said it was the first meeting where she felt heard.
I still use my laptop all day. Just not when someone is talking to me.

qa.q: How long did Kunal cut the meeting to?
qa.a: Kunal cut the meeting to twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Kunal feel watching six lit faces in the meeting?
qa.a: Kunal felt uneasy and frustrated, seeing everyone half there and nothing getting decided.

qa.q: What rule did Kunal set, and why did it work?
qa.a: Laptops closed and phones face down except for the note-taker, with short meetings and permission to skip, so people gave full attention and decided faster.

qa.q: How did Farida feel after the change?
qa.a: Farida said it was the first meeting where she felt heard.

grounding: Shows a young team lead who notices colleagues half-listening while typing and sets a norm of full attention for short meetings.

Our weekly review has been dragging. Today I watched instead of talking. Dhruv presented his new layout for fifteen minutes. Four of the five people listening had laptops open and were answering emails. When Dhruv asked for feedback, there was a long silence, then one person said, "Looks good," without really looking.

What I did next: from next week, reviews will be thirty minutes, not ninety. Laptops closed, except the one on the projector. Each person gives one specific comment. If someone must answer an urgent email, they can step out and come back.
I'll try it for a month and then ask the team whether it's better.

qa.a: Thirty-minute reviews with laptops closed except the projector and one specific comment each, so people give full attention to the work.

After Christmas at his grandparents' house in Toledo, Bilal told the story to his uncle Javier. "We had a big dinner, and I got a train set."
Two days later, telling his teacher, it was: "We had a big dinner, I got a train set, and it snowed." It hadn't snowed.
By New Year, telling a friend: "It snowed, and a reindeer looked in the window!"
Javier smiled. "Bilal, did you really see a reindeer?"
Bilal thought hard. "Yes," he said, completely sure. "Like in my book."
Javier didn't argue. He remembered the book on Bilal's bed: a Christmas story with snow and a reindeer at the window.

qa.a: Bilal got a train set.

qa.q: Why was Bilal completely sure he saw a reindeer?
qa.a: Bilal felt sure and excited, because each retelling blended in pictures from his Christmas book until they felt like real memories.

qa.q: What did Javier do that was wise?
qa.a: Javier didn't argue, noticing that the book on Bilal's bed explained where the snow and the reindeer came from.

qa.q: How might Bilal's teacher hear the story?
qa.a: The teacher probably heard a lovely Christmas story, not knowing some parts came from a book.

grounding: Shows a preschooler whose Christmas story grows with each retelling as details from a storybook become part of the memory.

After the summer trip to Ooty, Jahnavi and her sister Swati told the story at every family dinner in their Chennai flat.
Swati's version always had the monkey. "It jumped on the car and stole Papa's sunglasses!"
By the third retelling, Jahnavi was telling it too. "I saw it! It had a baby on its back, and it grinned at me."
At Diwali, their grandmother looked through the trip photos. "Jahnavi, where were you when the monkey came?"
"In the car, watching."
Papa laughed. "You were asleep, kanna. You slept through the whole thing. Swati woke you afterwards."
Jahnavi stared at him. She could see the monkey, the baby, the grin. It felt exactly like a memory.
"But I remember it," she said quietly.

qa.q: What did the monkey steal?
qa.a: The monkey stole Papa's sunglasses.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi feel sure she saw the monkey?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt confident, because hearing Swati's version again and again had rebuilt the memory until it felt like her own.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi learn from this?
qa.a: That memories are rebuilt each time they're told, so photos or others' accounts can help check what really happened.

qa.q: How did Papa see Jahnavi's version?
qa.a: Papa found it funny and affectionate, knowing she had slept through the whole thing.

grounding: Shows a child who absorbs details from a sister's retelling of a family trip and believes she saw them herself.

Last Diwali we went to our village, and I've told the story so many times since. I'm Hrithik. In my first version, a cow walked into Dadi's kitchen and ate a roti. That's true, I think.
But my little brother Pranav tells it with the cow eating a whole plate of laddoos. After a few weeks, I started telling it that way too. Then I added that the cow looked at me and winked. I was sure it winked.
This summer, Dadi showed us a video she had taken. The cow walked in, sniffed a basket of onions and walked out. No roti. No laddoos. No wink.
I felt weird watching it. I could still see the wink in my head.
Now I know memories aren't like videos. Every time I tell a story, I sort of build it again, and sometimes I build it wrong.

qa.q: What did Hrithik learn about memory, and how could it help?
qa.a: That each retelling rebuilds the story, sometimes wrongly, so checking a video or asking others can help.
